newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian troops continue patrol in Kalimantan.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian troops continue patrol in Kalimantan.

text.p: Indonesian troops are guarding several towns in West Kalimantan province as calm gradually returns after ethnic riots since late December, military officials and residents said on Saturday.
"Soldiers are still guarding the towns in the interior. The overall situation is under control," a military official told Reuters from Pontianak, capital of West Kalimantan.

The official said traditional ceremonies to ease tension had been held in several places in the interior between the native Dayak and the people from Madura island, off the main Indonesian island of Java.
"The government has planned to organise the ceremony in Pontianak, but it still unclear when," he said.

Trouble erupted in the province bordering Malaysia's Sarawak state in what police said was a fight between Dayak and Maduran youths over a girl at a concert in Sanggau Ledo, about 95 km (60 miles) north of Pontianak.
The fighting spread to other parts of the province. In Sanggau, 140 km (90 miles) east of Pontianak, Maduran families have taken refuge in army camps after a series of fights between the two groups.
Residents in Pontianak said on Saturday that business activity was normal and threatening behaviour by Madurans towards Dayaks had stopped.

The Merdeka newspaper quoted Major-General Namuri Anoem, head of the Tanjungpura military command that oversees Kalimantan's four provinces, as saying on Thursday that 68 people had been arrested for their involvement in the riots.
The official Antara news agency quoted army chief of staff General Raden Hartono as saying on Friday that many people were victims of the Dayak-Madura riots since late December.
Diplomatic sources said it appeared that in some cases, soldiers had fired in self-defence.
Most Dayaks are Christians while the Maduran migrants are Moslems, like most Indonesians. At least 19 people have died in religious and ethnic riots in Indonesia since October.
The military and residents in the province say at least 12 people have died over the past six weeks. Some residents and church sources say the figure could be much higher.
